unit_label: BFM Module C unit 2 (courseware unit 20): treasury products

facts.statement: Foreign exchange market features (courseware): free currencies (major, fully convertible) can be readily bought and sold; the Indian rupee is partially convertible but the USD/INR market is fairly liquid owing to the large domestic market. Features: a transparent market (most transactions on-line, rates reflected on screens even when trades occur in New York or Tokyo); a virtual market with no physical boundaries, limited only by domestic regulation or convertibility; fast information through electronic media and vendor screens; and a liquid market open 24 hours across time zones with the largest trading volume. It is near perfect with an efficient price discovery mechanism; dealers offer two-way quotes (simultaneous purchase and sale), giving liquidity and transparency; the narrower the buy-sell spread, the more liquid the currency.

Spot and forward markets (courseware): a spot trade settles two working days from the trade date (value spot); a currency may also be traded for settlement the same day (TOD/Cash) or the next day (TOM). Rates quoted on screen are for spot by default. TOD and TOM rates are generally quoted at a discount to spot; in an integrated market the premium or discount is decided by demand and supply of the base currency and overnight interest rate differentials. A forward transaction is a purchase or sale of a currency on a future date at a rate quoted today; customers (importers, exporters) cover exposure by forward contracts with banks, and Treasury covers its exposure by opposite positions in the inter-bank market or takes forward positions for proprietary profit. Forward rates are not forecasts of future rates; they are derived from interest rate differentials of two currencies, added to or deducted from the spot rate: the difference between spot and forward reflects the difference in risk-free interest rates of the two currencies.

Forward rate determination and NDFs (courseware): the interest rate differential is added to the spot rate for the low-interest yielding currency (representing forward premium) and deducted from the spot rate for the high-interest yielding currency (forward discount). Forward rates fully reflect interest rate differentials only in perfect markets where currencies are fully convertible and markets are highly liquid; because the rupee is not fully convertible, demand and supply of foreign currency in the forward tenor also influence the forward rates. A non-deliverable forward (NDF) is a forward contract traded over the counter at offshore centres, cash settled in an international currency on a specified future date without physical delivery of the currencies; it evolved for non-convertible currencies and remains outside the regulatory purview of the local authorities. NDF participants include foreign investors hedging, hedge funds, banks and speculators; they let agents facing onshore restrictions hedge or take positions, and efforts have focused on improving access to onshore markets.

Futures, options and swaps (courseware): a futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a certain price at a certain time; unlike a forward (over the counter), it is traded on an exchange with standardised size and maturity, initial and variation margins are maintained with the exchange and positions are normally closed out by opposite trades; the exchange guarantees settlement so counterparty risk is absent. An option gives the buyer (holder) the right but not the obligation to buy or sell a specified quantity of the underlying at a strike price on or before expiry; an American option can be exercised any time up to expiry, a European option only on the expiry date. A call gives the holder the right to buy (the seller or writer has the obligation to sell if exercised); a put gives the right to sell (the seller has the obligation to buy). A swap is a combination of spot and forward transactions, or of two forwards: buying USD spot and selling the same amount forward (or the reverse) is a USD/INR swap; forward-to-forward is also a swap. Swaps are used for funding and interest arbitrage (for example selling USD spot to get rupees for a three-month commercial paper investment and buying back the USD forward: the cost of USD funds is the market rate plus forward premium; profit if the CP return exceeds it). Interest arbitrage exists only when currencies are not fully convertible; between free currencies the forward premium equals the interest differential. Currency swaps convert cash flows from principal and interest in one currency to another, distinct from short-term funding swaps.

Investment of foreign exchange surpluses and related products (courseware): surpluses arise from treasury profits, overseas branch operations, foreign currency borrowings and foreign currency and convertible rupee deposits with branches (mainly from non-resident depositors and exporters), including float funds on customer transactions (nostro balances, EEFC balances) and rupee funds swapped into foreign currency. Avenues: inter-bank loans (normally up to one year but mostly overnight deposits with domestic and global banks within pre-approved limits), short-term investments in high credit quality instruments (treasury bills, commercial paper and other debt of multilateral institutions and companies with AAA rating) under a board-approved policy, and nostro accounts, which earn no interest but many correspondent banks offer automatic investment facilities for funds held overnight above a minimum balance (a sweep facility) with interest linked to the central bank rate of the currency. Treasury is not involved in credit appraisal but is consulted on the availability and cost of foreign currency funds for foreign currency loans: loans funded by foreign currency non-resident deposits, packing credit in foreign currency, discounting foreign bills; Treasury is more involved in short-term funding. Rediscounting of foreign bills: an inter-bank advance where Treasury refinances foreign bills negotiated by another bank, without recourse to the customer, priced higher than money market placements, with a usance of 15 to 360 days, the counterparty charging its customer the commercial rate; the lending bank has the borrowing bank as counterparty. Money markets and foreign exchange fund management overlap.

Money market and inter-bank instruments (courseware): the money market is for raising and deploying short-term resources with maturity not exceeding one year. The inter-bank market consists of call money (overnight placements, repaid the next working day), notice money (funds for 2 to 14 days) and term money (placements for more than 14 days and up to one year; typically one to six months). All three are unsecured. The overnight Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate (O/N MIBOR) is the indicative rate for call money, fixed daily and widely used as benchmark for overnight rate swaps and floating rate paper. Non-bank participants were phased out of call money (2005). Prudential limits are decided by the board within the exposure norms of the central bank and differ by participant type (details not taught). The inter-bank market carries the lowest credit risk, next only to sovereign risk, so it signals changes in money supply and liquidity; the call rate is a benchmark. Treasury invests surplus cash in the money market after meeting CRR and SLR; the central bank pays no interest on CRR balances. Bank treasuries deal in inter-bank markets and also in short-term paper issued by government, financial institutions and companies.

Treasury bills and cash management bills (courseware): treasury bills (T-bills) are issued by the government through the central bank for maturities of 91, 182 and 364 days at a discount to face value (interest is the discount), through auctions in which banks and primary dealers are the main participants but others can bid; non-competitive bids are allowed for specified entities and retail investors. Yield (implicit yield) = (100 - price) / price x (365 / days to maturity); the courseware example: a 91-day bill priced at 99.26 yields (100 - 99.26) / 99.26 x 365 / 91 = 2.99 per cent. T-bills are a risk-free investment, liquid in the secondary market, and a benchmark for debt paper; they are held in electronic form in an SGL account (subsidiary general ledger at the central bank), settlement of secondary market trades by the clearing corporation, and they are redeemed at par on the previous working day if maturity falls on a holiday. Cash management bills (CMBs) are non-standard discounted instruments for maturities under 91 days issued to meet temporary cash flow mismatches of the government; the tenure and amount depend on its cash needs, they are issued by auction at a discount with T+1 settlement, are tradable and eligible for repo, and count as an SLR investment.

Commercial paper and certificates of deposit (courseware): commercial paper (CP) is a short-term unsecured promissory note issued by corporates and other eligible entities at a discount to face value (priced for a face value of Rs 100), negotiable, issued in demat form through an issuing and paying agent which must be a scheduled bank; the issuer must meet a minimum credit rating and net worth and be a standard asset (conditions not taught), with a minimum maturity of 7 days and a maximum of one year and a minimum amount of Rs 5 lakh and multiples; every issue or renewal is a fresh issue; trades are reported to a trade reporting platform within 15 minutes; settlement T+0 or T+1. CP carries relatively low credit risk (short term, minimum rating) and is used by issuers as a substitute for bank working capital at rates below bank lending rates. The CP return is generally higher than the inter-bank money market yield and CP is tradable with lesser liquidity than T-bills. Buyback: the issuer can buy back CP before maturity in the secondary market at prevailing price, not within a minimum period of 30 days of issue. Certificates of deposit (CDs) are unsecured negotiable instruments issued by banks (or eligible financial institutions) against funds deposited at a discount to face value, with interest rates generally higher than regular deposits; meant for high net worth individuals (minimum amount Rs 5 lakh); tenor of 7 days to 1 year for banks (1 to 3 years for financial institutions); they attract stamp duty, so are more expensive; banks maintain CRR and SLR on the issue price; banks cannot lend against CDs or permit premature closure; secondary market is not very active; banks may buy back CDs after seven days, and repurchased CDs must be extinguished. Details, amounts and tenors are not taught.

Market repo and TREPS (courseware): repo is a securities transaction used for lending and borrowing money market funds (1 day to 1 year): the seller (borrower) sells securities and commits to repurchase them at a later date at a pre-agreed price; the difference between sale and repurchase price is the interest on the cash. The counterparty obtains secured lending and holds securities that help meet SLR. The effective interest on repo is generally lower than the corresponding money market rate since the lender holds securities. The legal form is a sale and repurchase, but accounting treats it as borrowing (book value unchanged); repo adjustments are routed through a repo price adjustment account to reflect the interest. A haircut (hair cut) is the margin by which the cash advanced is lower than the market value of securities to cover price risk; it depends on repo period, riskiness of the securities and coupon. Repo can be in central and state government securities and listed corporate bonds; repo borrowing in government securities is exempt from CRR/SLR computation; the lender in a repo with corporate bonds also bears issuer credit risk. Settlement of repos in government securities is through the clearing corporation; repos are reported to trading and reporting platforms. Tri-party repo (TREPS, replaced the earlier collateralised borrowing and lending obligation) has a third entity (the clearing corporation as tri-party agent) between borrower and lender providing collateral selection, payment and settlement, custody and management; it offers novation (the clearing corporation becomes the common counterparty), net settlement and initial and mark-to-market margin; tenors from one day to one year; eligible participants include regulated entities and listed corporates.

Liquidity adjustment facility and corridor (courseware): the central bank uses repo as a monetary policy instrument under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF): repo is a liquidity injection (banks sell government securities to the central bank with a commitment to repurchase) and reverse repo absorbs excess liquidity (banks buy securities with an agreement to resell); the repo rate is the rate for borrowing from the central bank and the reverse repo rate the rate for lending to it; these are policy rates and set the ceiling and floor of the call money market (the corridor). Fixed rate overnight and variable rate repo and reverse repo are used, with auctions of different tenors. The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), operational from April 2022, lets banks place deposits with the central bank overnight without collateral and replaces the fixed rate reverse repo as the floor, at 25 basis points below the policy repo rate; SDF balances are not reckoned as CRR but are eligible for SLR. The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), introduced in 2011, lets banks borrow overnight against government securities, including those within the SLR requirement (up to a limit of net demand and time liabilities), at a rate above the repo rate (the ceiling of the corridor). The interest rate corridor is the policy framework guiding money market rates within a defined range: SDF rate (floor), policy repo rate (middle) and MSF rate (ceiling). The rates, limits and timings in the courseware are as at 2022 and are not taught.

Bill rediscounting and securities market products (courseware): bill rediscounting is investment of money market funds by discounting bills of exchange of short tenor (3 to 6 months) at around money market rate; credit risk is low since the bills carry the borrowing bank co-acceptance, and the borrowing bank gets liquidity and improves its capital adequacy as the bills are taken out of the credit portfolio. Government securities (G-secs) are issued by the central bank for the government (and state development loans for state governments) through auctions; interest is a coupon on the face value (minimum Rs 10,000) with price determined by the auction; price and yield are inversely related; the yield to maturity depends on the coupon, price and time (example type: a 5.85 per cent bond priced at 98.90 has a yield of 6.00 per cent). The central bank is the issuing and paying agent, and uses G-secs for open market operations (selling to absorb liquidity, buying to inject it). Treasury invests in G-secs for SLR and for profit from price changes: the price-yield relation is inverse, and interest rate views depend on inflation, GDP growth and other indicators. SLR is a percentage of net demand and time liabilities held in approved securities, controlled by the central bank (subject to a statutory ceiling; the courseware gives its history); banks may also hold cash or gold to fulfil it. Classification of investments: Held to Maturity (banking book), Available for Sale and Held for Trading (trading book, marked to market regularly); AFS must be marked to market at least quarterly. STRIPS are separate zero-coupon securities from principal and interest. Details not taught.

Corporate debt, debentures and bonds, convertible bonds (courseware): corporate debt paper (non-SLR securities) is medium and long-term bonds and debentures issued by corporates and financial institutions, tradable, yielding more than government securities because of credit risk (the higher the risk, the higher the yield); most issues are rated by registered credit rating agencies; global ratings are needed for international issues; banks may invest only in demat securities. Debentures and bonds are debt instruments, with or without security; in India debentures are conventionally issued by private companies and bonds by public sector entities (not implying a government guarantee), and in practice the distinction is minimal; the term bond is used generally for non-convertible corporate debt of original maturity of one year or above. Variations to improve marketability or lower cost: structured obligations with put/call or convertibility, zero coupon bonds (issued at a deep discount), floating rate bonds (coupon linked to a benchmark reset periodically), deep discount bonds (interest only at maturity), step-up coupons, period bonds (redeemed in instalments), collateralised obligations, and bonds with put call options and step up coupons. Bond holders have a prior claim over equity and preference holders; a trustee acts for the holders under a trust deed. Convertible bonds are a mix of debt and equity with an option to convert into equity at a predetermined price or formula; holders convert if the stock price is above the conversion price; the benefit to the company is no debt repayment and stronger equity base, with a lower coupon than a non-convertible bond but dilution if converted.

Equities and domestic-global market links (courseware): banks may invest in equities of listed companies subject to central bank limits on capital market exposure (the courseware states 40 per cent of net worth overall and 20 per cent direct, and 30 per cent of the share capital of an investee company or of capital plus reserves; guarantees to stockbrokers are indirect exposure; figures not taught). Share capital is equity or preference; preference shares may be cumulative or non-cumulative, redeemable or irredeemable (irredeemable preference shares are prohibited by the Companies Act as stated), participating or non-participating, and convertible or non-convertible. Equity prices depend on fundamentals and macroeconomic factors, so treasuries are cautious, and equity is an important part of the portfolio. The domestic and global markets interact through: foreign investment (foreign direct investment and portfolio investment by foreign institutional investors; the latter fluctuates with the market); ADR/GDR issues by Indian companies (receipts for shares sold to foreign investors, with the exchange risk borne by the overseas investor); external commercial borrowings (borrowing from foreign lenders or bonds; the exchange risk is borne by the Indian borrower); foreign currency funds of banks (foreign currency non-resident deposit funds invested overseas or lent at home within ceilings); special facilities for exporters (EEFC accounts, pre- and post-shipment credit in foreign currency); overseas direct investment by Indian corporates; and the liberalised remittance facility for individuals. Two-way capital flows affect interest rates and exchange rates (the 2007 appreciation and the 2008-09 depreciation and policy response are narrative). Close interaction means globalisation is not an unmixed blessing: adequate safety measures are needed, and the 2008-09 crisis showed systemic risk.

payload.title: Features of the foreign exchange market
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Free (fully convertible) currencies** can be bought and sold readily. The rupee is **partially convertible**, but the **USD/INR market is fairly liquid** because of the large domestic market.

**Features:** **transparent** (on-line rates across time zones), **virtual** (no physical boundaries; limited only by domestic regulation or convertibility), **fast information** through electronic screens, and **liquid and open around the clock** with the largest trading volume of any market.

Dealers give **two-way quotes** (buy and sell together). The **narrower the buy-sell spread, the more liquid** the currency.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Two-way quotes let a customer deal at once without revealing whether they buy or sell.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a narrow buy-sell spread indicate?

payload.title: Spot market and value dates
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **spot** trade settles **two working days after the trade date**. Other value dates: **TOD/Cash** (same day) and **TOM** (next day). Rates on the screen are **spot by default**.

TOD and TOM rates are generally quoted at a **discount to spot** in the courseware, but in an integrated market the premium or discount depends on **demand and supply of the base currency** and **overnight interest rate differentials**, so the sign can vary.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Value date is the date on which the currency amounts actually change hands.

self_check.prompt_text: When does a spot trade settle?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Two working days after the trade date.

payload.title: Forward market and how forward rates arise
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **forward** buys or sells a currency on a **future date** at a **rate fixed today**. Customers (importers, exporters) **cover exposure** with forwards; Treasury covers by taking **opposite positions** in the inter-bank market or takes forward positions for **proprietary profit**.

**Forward rates are not forecasts.** They come from the **interest rate differential** of the two currencies: the differential is **added to spot for the low-interest currency (forward premium)** and **deducted from spot for the high-interest currency (forward discount)**.

They match the differential **only in perfect markets** with full convertibility and liquidity. Because the rupee is not fully convertible, **demand and supply of foreign currency** in the forward tenor also affect rupee forward rates.

**NDF (non-deliverable forward):** an **OTC forward traded offshore**, **cash settled in an international currency** with **no physical delivery**; it arose for **non-convertible currencies** and sits **outside local regulatory purview**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The currency with the lower interest rate trades at a forward premium.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a forward rate a forecast of the future spot rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it is derived from the interest rate differential and the spot rate.

payload.title: Forward rate from interest rate parity
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Forward = Spot x (1 + r_quote x n/365) / (1 + r_base x n/365)**, where **r_quote** is the interest rate of the **quoted currency** (rupee) and **r_base** that of the **base currency** (dollar), over **n days**.

**Annualised premium (per cent) = (Forward - Spot) / Spot x 365 / n x 100.**

If the quoted (rupee) rate is **higher** than the dollar rate, the dollar is at a **forward premium** against the rupee.

Perfect-market simplification used in the courseware: the **swap points are about the interest differential** applied to spot.

formula_spec.latex_expression: F = S \times \frac{1 + r_q \, n/365}{1 + r_b \, n/365}

variables.name: Interest rate of the quoted currency
Interest rate of the base currency

assumptions: Simple interest on a 365 day year

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Rupee forwards can differ from this value because of forward demand and supply.

self_check.prompt_text: Which currency is at a forward premium?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The one with the lower interest rate.

payload.title: Futures, options and swaps
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Instrument | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| **Futures** | **Exchange traded**, **standardised** size and maturity, **initial and variation margin**, usually **closed out by an opposite trade**, **exchange guarantees settlement** so **no counterparty risk** |
| **Forward** | **Over the counter**, tailored |
| **Option** | **Right, not obligation**, to buy or sell at a **strike** on or before expiry; **American** (any time to expiry) or **European** (expiry only) |
| **Call** | Holder may **buy**; the **writer must sell** if exercised |
| **Put** | Holder may **sell**; the **writer must buy** |
| **Swap** | **Spot plus forward** (buy USD spot and sell forward, or the reverse) or **forward-to-forward** |

**Swap for funding:** sell USD spot for rupees to invest in a three-month CP and buy USD forward: the **cost of USD funds = market rate + forward premium**; profit if the **CP return exceeds** it. **Interest arbitrage exists only when currencies are not fully convertible**; between free currencies the forward premium **equals the interest differential**. **Currency swaps** exchange cash flows in two currencies and differ from short-term funding swaps.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The seller of an option bears the obligation; the buyer pays a premium for the right.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is counterparty risk absent in exchange traded futures?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The exchange guarantees settlement between the parties.

payload.title: Investing foreign exchange surpluses; loans and rediscounting
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Sources of surplus:** **treasury profits**, **overseas branch operations**, **foreign currency borrowings** and **foreign currency and convertible rupee deposits** (mainly NRI and exporters), including **float funds** such as nostro and EEFC balances.

**Avenues:**

- **Inter-bank loans** (mostly **overnight**, within pre-approved limits).
- **Short-term investments** in **high-quality paper** (treasury bills, CP and debt of multilaterals and AAA companies) under a **board policy**.
- **Nostro accounts** earn **no interest**, but a **sweep facility** invests balances above a minimum overnight and pays interest linked to the central bank rate of that currency.

**Loans and advances:** Treasury does **no credit appraisal** but is consulted on **availability and cost of foreign currency funds** (FCNR-funded loans, packing credit, discounting foreign bills).

**Rediscounting of foreign bills:** an **inter-bank advance** refinancing bills negotiated by another bank, **without recourse to the customer**, priced **above money market placements**, tenor **15 to 360 days**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A sweep facility turns idle overnight balances into interest-bearing placements.

self_check.prompt_text: Does a nostro account earn interest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Normally no, unless an automatic investment (sweep) facility is used.

payload.title: Inter-bank money market: call, notice and term money
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **money market** raises and deploys funds with maturity **not over one year**.

| Instrument | Tenor |
| --- | --- |
| **Call money** | **Overnight**; repaid the **next working day** |
| **Notice money** | **2 to 14 days** |
| **Term money** | **More than 14 days up to one year** (usually 1 to 6 months) |

All are **unsecured**. **O/N MIBOR** (overnight Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate) is the **indicative call rate**, used as a **benchmark** for floating rate paper and overnight swaps.

The inter-bank market has the **lowest credit risk after sovereign risk**, so it signals **money supply and liquidity**. Treasury invests surplus **after meeting CRR and SLR**; **no interest is paid on CRR balances**. Prudential limits vary by participant and are not taught.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Call money is the shortest and most liquid inter-bank rate.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Funds placed between banks for 2 to 14 days.

payload.title: Treasury bills: discount, price and yield
payload.core_explanation_md:
T-bills are issued at a **discount**; the discount is the interest. Tenors: **91, 182 and 364 days**.

**Implicit yield = (100 - price) / price x (365 / days) x 100.**

Example pattern: a **91-day bill at 99.26**: (0.74 / 99.26) x (365 / 91) = **2.99 per cent**.

**Price = 100 / (1 + yield x days / 365).**

T-bills are **risk-free**, **liquid**, a **benchmark**, held in an **SGL account** and **redeemed at par** the previous working day if maturity falls on a holiday.

**Cash management bills (CMBs):** **under 91 days**, issued for the **government short-term cash needs**, by auction at a discount, **T+1 settlement**, tradable, repo-eligible, count towards **SLR**.

common_errors: Dividing by 100 instead of the price

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because the yield is on the price paid, not on the face value, it is higher than the discount rate.

self_check.expected_takeaway: As a discount: the bill is issued below face value and redeemed at par.

payload.title: Commercial paper and certificates of deposit
payload.core_explanation_md:
| | **Commercial paper (CP)** | **Certificate of deposit (CD)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Issuer** | **Corporates and other eligible entities** | **Banks** (and eligible financial institutions) |
| **Nature** | **Unsecured promissory note**, negotiable, **discount to face value** | **Unsecured negotiable** deposit instrument at a discount |
| **Form** | **Demat**, through an **issuing and paying agent** (a scheduled bank) | Demat or promissory note |
| **Tenor** | **7 days to 1 year** | **7 days to 1 year** (banks); **1 to 3 years** (FIs) |
| **Minimum** | Rs 5 lakh and multiples | Rs 5 lakh (high net worth focus) |
| **Key points** | **Low credit risk**, **cheaper than bank working capital**, yields **above inter-bank money** and **less liquid than T-bills**; **buyback** allowed after a minimum period | **Rates above regular deposits**; **stamp duty** makes it costlier; **CRR and SLR** apply on issue price; **no loans against CDs**, **no premature closure**; **buyback after seven days** and extinguished |

OTC trades are **reported within 15 minutes**; settlement **T+0 or T+1** (CP). Eligibility, ratings, amounts and tenors vary by rule and are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: CP lets a good-credit company borrow below the bank lending rate.

self_check.prompt_text: Who issues commercial paper and who issues certificates of deposit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Corporates and other eligible entities issue CP; banks and eligible financial institutions issue CDs.

payload.title: Market repo and tri-party repo (TREPS)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Repo** is a **sale and repurchase**: the borrower **sells securities** and **agrees to buy them back** later at a **pre-agreed price**; the **price difference is the interest**. The lender gets **secured lending** and securities that can help meet **SLR**. Effective repo rates are generally **below the money market rate** since the lender holds collateral. **Accounting treats it as borrowing**; the security stays at book value; a **repo price adjustment account** reflects the interest.

**Haircut:** the **margin** by which the cash advanced is **below the market value** of securities, covering **price risk**; it depends on **period, riskiness and coupon**.

- Repo in **government securities** settles through the **clearing corporation**; repo borrowing in government securities is exempt from CRR/SLR computation.
- In **corporate bond repo** the lender also bears **issuer credit risk**.

**TREPS:** a **tri-party agent** (the clearing corporation) between borrower and lender handles **collateral selection, payment, settlement, custody and management**, provides **novation** (it becomes the common counterparty) and **net settlement**, and takes **initial and mark-to-market margin**. Tenors **1 day to 1 year**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A larger haircut means the lender advances less against the same collateral.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a haircut in a repo?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The margin by which cash lent is below the market value of the collateral, covering price risk.

payload.title: Repo interest, haircut and cash advanced
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Cash advanced = market value of securities x (1 - haircut).**

**Repurchase price = cash x (1 + repo rate x days / 365).**

**Interest = repurchase price - cash advanced.**

Example pattern: securities **Rs 100 crore**, haircut **5 per cent**: cash **Rs 95 crore**; at **6 per cent for 7 days** the interest is **95 x 0.06 x 7 / 365 = Rs 0.109 crore**.

common_errors: Charging interest on the market value

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Interest is charged on cash lent, not on the value of the collateral.

self_check.prompt_text: On what amount is repo interest charged?
self_check.expected_takeaway: On the cash advanced, not on the market value of the securities.

payload.title: Liquidity adjustment facility, SDF, MSF and the corridor
payload.core_explanation_md:
The central bank manages liquidity through the **liquidity adjustment facility (LAF)**:

- **Repo** = banks **borrow** against government securities: **injects liquidity**. The **repo rate** is the rate for borrowing.
- **Reverse repo** = banks **lend** to the central bank: **absorbs liquidity**.

| Facility | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** | **Overnight deposits with the central bank without collateral**; **replaces fixed rate reverse repo as the floor**; rate **25 basis points below the policy repo**; **not counted as CRR** but eligible for **SLR** |
| **Policy repo rate** | The **middle** of the corridor |
| **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** | **Overnight borrowing against government securities** (including SLR securities, up to a limit of NDTL), at a rate **above the repo rate**: the **ceiling** |

The **interest rate corridor** (**SDF floor, repo middle, MSF ceiling**) guides money market rates, so that overnight call rates stay within it. Rates, limits and timings in the courseware are as at 2022 and are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The MSF is a safety valve for banks short of funds; the SDF is a parking place for surplus.

self_check.prompt_text: Which facility sets the floor of the corridor and which the ceiling?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Standing Deposit Facility is the floor and the Marginal Standing Facility is the ceiling.

payload.title: Bill rediscounting and government securities
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Bill rediscounting:** discounting bills of exchange (**3 to 6 months**) at about the money market rate; **low credit risk** because bills carry the **borrowing bank co-acceptance**. The borrowing bank gets **liquidity** and improves **capital adequacy** as bills leave its credit portfolio.

**Government securities (G-secs):** issued by the central bank for the government (**state development loans** for states) by **auction**. Interest is a **coupon on face value**; the price is set by the auction. **Price and yield move in opposite directions.**

**Uses by Treasury:** **SLR** holdings and **profit from price changes**. **SLR** is a percentage of **net demand and time liabilities** held in approved securities (or cash or gold), subject to a statutory ceiling. The central bank also uses G-secs for **open market operations**: **selling absorbs liquidity**, **buying injects** it.

**Classification:** **HTM** (banking book), **AFS** (**marked to market at least quarterly**) and **HFT** (trading book, **marked to market regularly**). **STRIPS** are separately traded **zero-coupon** pieces of principal and interest.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: When market interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall.

payload.title: Corporate debt, debentures, bonds and convertibles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Corporate debt paper** (non-SLR securities) is **medium and long-term bonds and debentures** of corporates and financial institutions: **tradable**, with a **higher yield than government securities** because of **credit risk** (**higher risk, higher yield**). Most are **rated** by registered agencies; **global ratings** are needed for international issues. Banks may invest only in **demat** form.

**Debentures and bonds:** conventionally debentures are issued by **private companies** and bonds by **public sector entities**, with **no government guarantee implied**; in practice the distinction is minor. Holders have a **prior claim over equity and preference holders**; a **trustee** acts for them under a **trust deed**.

**Structures:** **zero coupon**, **floating rate** (coupon reset against a benchmark), **deep discount** (interest at maturity), **step-up coupon**, **period bonds** (redeemed in instalments), **put/call options**.

**Convertible bonds:** debt with an **option to convert into equity** at a **predetermined price or formula**; holders convert if the **share price is above the conversion price**. For the company: **no repayment** and a **stronger equity base**, **lower coupon**, but **dilution**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A convertible gives investors upside in return for accepting a lower coupon.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do corporate bonds yield more than government securities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They carry credit risk, which investors are paid to bear.

payload.title: Equities and the links between domestic and global markets
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Equities:** banks may invest in **listed company shares** within central bank **capital market exposure limits** (limits on overall exposure, direct exposure, and share of an investee company; **guarantees to stockbrokers** are **indirect exposure**; figures not taught). **Preference shares** may be **cumulative or non-cumulative**, **redeemable or irredeemable**, **participating or non-participating**, **convertible or not**. Equity prices depend on **fundamentals and macroeconomic factors**, so treasuries are cautious.

**Links between domestic and global markets:**

| Link | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Foreign investment** | **FDI** (long term) and **FII portfolio** flows (fluctuate with markets) |
| **ADR/GDR** | Indian company **sells receipts for shares** abroad; **overseas investor bears exchange risk** |
| **ECB** | Indian company **borrows abroad**; **borrower bears exchange risk** |
| **Banks foreign currency funds** | **FCNR funds** invested overseas or lent at home within ceilings |
| **Exporters** | **EEFC accounts**, **pre- and post-shipment credit in foreign currency** |
| **ODI** | **Indian corporates invest overseas** |
| **Liberalised remittance facility** | **Individuals remit abroad** within a limit |

Two-way flows affect **interest and exchange rates**; **globalisation is not an unmixed blessing**: the 2008-09 crisis showed **systemic risk**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Who bears the exchange risk differs between ADR/GDR (investor) and ECB (borrower).

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk on an ADR or GDR, and who on an ECB?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The overseas investor on an ADR or GDR; the Indian borrower on an ECB.
